author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter reached me at the Malmaison. I desire that the conference should not degenerate into a conversation. Show yourself cold, haughty, and even somewhat proud. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Amiens ruptured: the truce is over, the invasion army rises.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The affairs of Ireland make me' feel the necessity of your having some private conferences with the chiefs of the United Irishmen now in Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you the despatch from Madrid of the 13th Fructidor. I am surprised that we have no other news. Make out a list of all the complaints we have against Spain, so that we may have materials ready in the event of requiring them.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you your despatches, Citizen Minister. Tell Citizen Laforest that I have read his despatch with great interest. It will be well to warn the Turkish ambassador that the English, who evidently encourage the Beys, intend to seize upon Egypt.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen General, — I have received your letter, and have given orders for hoods to be served out to all the men forming part of the expedition to Ireland, of which you shall have the command. Affairs are settled with Spain and Portugal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Boulogne camps: invasion of England prepared.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “For the last week we have been in pursuit of forty brigands composed of Georges and his band, who disembarked at three different places. Another band is to disembark; we have arrested all the men who were to make signals. Savary awaits them at Biville. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Camp of Boulogne: Soult drills the invasion army.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Due d'Enghien is to be taken to the castle of Vincennes, where arrangements have been made for his reception. The First Consul desires that the name of this prisoner, and everything concerning him, may be kept secret. he travels under the name of Plessis. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Murat governs Paris as the Enghien crisis breaks.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I thank your Holiness for having given a cardinal's hat to the Archbishop of Bologna. I have come to the determination to take into my own hands all that relates to the Concordat with the Italian Republic. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Steube, the minister of Wirtemberg, is a downright fool, as ill-meaning as ignorant. If you can insinuate in a delicate manner that he ought to be recalled, that would please me. " Write to General Lannes at Lisbon, and mention the matter to M. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I desire that the official note of Lord Hawkesbury may be sent to all our agents at foreign courts, those of Russia, Sweden, Denmark, and the Porte excepted, with remarks to this effect — that the French Government calls attention to the note in question; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But for this miserable trial [of Moreau, &c.] I should be in the midst of the camps. I hope everything will be finished in a week. I suppose that in camp as. well as in Paris there are rumours of a continental war. This would be unfortunate, as it would turn our attention from England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I desire that you will give me by return of post some information on the subject of the family of the Elector of Bavaria, especially concerning his daughter, and his intentions with regard to that young princess. I need hardly remind you that an affair of this nature must be kept perfectly secret. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madam and dear Wife, — For the last four days since I have been absent from you I have been constantly on horseback, and this exercise has not impaired my health. " M. Maret tells me that you intend starting on Monday. Travelling by easy stages you will be able to reach the waters without fatigue. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “D'Oubril has gone. Although this departure is not good news, still it does not mean a rupture; but it is incalculable what may happen within two or three months. "Napoleon." And on the same day Fouche was ordered not to allow any Russians to leave Paris without haying paid their debts. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Most Holy Father, — The happy effect which the re-establishment of the Christian religion has had on the morality and character of my people induces me to ask your Holiness to give a new proof of the interest you take in my destiny, and in that of this great nation, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “What happens at Bordeaux happens at Turin, at Spa, at Marseilles, &c. The police commissioners derive immense profits from the gaming-tables. My intention is that the towns shall reap the benefit of the tables. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Uncle and Cousin, — General Cafferelli is the bearer of the enclosed letter for the Pope. The Holy Father will travel in his own carriages to the foot of Mont Cenis; arrived there, my carriages will bring him on. All his expenses will be paid from the moment he sets foot in France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I arrive at Treves at the same time that you arrive at St. Cloud. Do not give an audience to T. Receive B. in public, and do not give him a private audience. Do not promise to sign any marriage contracts before they have been signed by me. "Napoleon." To M. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: On the road to the coronation.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will see in the Moniteiir of to-morrow an account of an unheard-of attack by the English on four Spanish frigates. Have several articles inserted in the papers with the object of exciting France to war, and of indisposing as much as possible the other Powers against England. SPANISH GALLEONS. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — I received your Majesty's letter this evening, and was much touched by the expressions of confidence and friendship which it contained. My first movement after reading your letter was to give orders for the immediate release of M. Rumbold. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Prussia, St.  Cloud, 1804-11-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I write you this letter to make known my displeasure in that you have permitted the word 'supper' to be used in the invitations of Wednesday, since the hour for which they are issued is that of my dinner. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Most high, most excellent, most powerful, most magnanimous and invincible prince, great Emperor of the Mussulmans, Sultan Selim, in whom honour and virtue abound, our very dear and perfect friend, may God augment your grandeur and r accord you a happy end. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Emperor of Turkey, Paris, 1805-01-30
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The present letter will be presented to your royal highness by General Junot, my ambassador. I have charged him specially to assure you of the interest I take in the welfare of Portugal, and the hopes I entertain that the two states will march together in order to attain that great result, […]”
sourceTitle: To the Prince Regent of Portugal, La  Malmaison, 1805-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A great many persons complain that classics are too dear. It would be well to appoint a commission to tax the price of books adopted by the lyceums at so much a page. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your courier has informed me of the capture of Dominica. My Toulon squadron sailed on the 9th (Germinal), or thirteen days ago, and I have no news of it. It had a division on board under the command of Lauriston. The English are in a bad way in India. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy armed for the coming war.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg you will inform M. de Moustier that I cannot conceive how a man of so much judgment allows 30,000 Russians to alarm him for Prussia which has 300,000 men. The artillery, cavalry, and officers of the Prussian army are worth thirty times those of Russia. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy beckons; the Boulogne army eyes east.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I forward you a report concerning Creusot. It is essential to keep up this establishment. It will not be well to purchase it; but I think it will be useful to give a fixed amount of orders, so that it may have a basis of operations, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother-in-law and Cousin, — What you write to me concerning the conclusion of a treaty of alliance between England and Russia is nonsense; it is entirely false. These reports, spread by the English so that they may for the moment escape from their difficulties, are unfounded. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Have several letters printed in the papers, as if from St. Petersburg, declaring that the French are much better treated; that court and town feel the necessity of making friends with us; that all are persuaded English avidity is the real cause of the war; that the English are unpopular; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The people of Genoa appear to desire their union to France. The advantages of this union, and circumstances, are such as to induce me to pay no attention to the blustering of a few Powers. In fact, this can excite the animadversion of England alone. To M. FOUCH. " Milan, 29 May, 1805. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “As nothing would give me a better idea of the exact feeling of the court of Vienna than a negotiation with the view of exchanging a certain number of cordons of the Legion of Honour against Austrian cordons, write to M. de la Rochefoucauld to tell M. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think I ordered you to embark everything, for circumstances may present themselves at any moment. I wish you to embark the artillery, powder, and all the ammunitions, so that in twenty-four bours the whole expedition may start. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Grande Armée staff work before the march.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have directed M. Marescalchi to forward you a de- ■ cree, ordering the Legislative Body to terminate its sittings. My intention is that during my reign in Italy it shall not meet again. I had too good an opinion of the Italians. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “All the news I receive from Italy is warlike, and Austria no longer conceals her intentions. Prepare a note for M. de Cobentzel, let it be long, wily, argumentative, and in similar terms to the inclosed. The note drawn up by Talleyrand was approved of, and forwarded to Vienna. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “As regards the encouragement of art, the Imperial Library being under the department. of the minister of the interior, and having placed 2oo,ooof. at his disposal,. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The camp breaks: administration turns toward the Rhine.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Sister, — I have ordered the grand marshal of my palace to send you my portrait, in accordance with your request, as you think it will be agreeable to the people of Lucca. Send me a detailed account of your coasts and a list of the batteries which are necessary. I will send you the guns. […]”
sourceTitle: To Princess Eliza, Camp  of  Boulogne, 1805-08-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The situation of my armies and the position of my forces do not permit of any transaction approaching to weakness. In giving Hanover to Prussia I give her a territory which will augment her forces to the extent of 40,000 men, and will also improve the situation of her states. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Boulogne to Rhine: the turn decided.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “With thirty vessels my admirals ought not to be afraid of twenty-four English ships, or else we must give up the idea of having a marine. If Villeneuve remains at Ferrol beyond the i6th, I shall consider him the last of men. According to the news from London, Nelson is still far away. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have arrived at Strasburg. All the army has passed the Rhine. The enemy is at the issues of the Black Forest. Our manoeuvres will soon commence. Do all you can to induce the nation to adopt the conscription. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Paris left to Joseph; the army marches.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Brother, — I have received your letter of the ist October. The King of Prussia never attached any importance to troops passing through Baireuth and Anspach. Our constant custom during the last war was to pass through the territory in question as often as we liked. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Elector of Bavaria, Ludwigsburg, 1805-10-02
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My good Josephine,— I have fatigued myself more than was prudent. All day long for a whole week wet to the skin, and the feet cold, have made me rather unwell; but I have not been out to-day, and that has rep'osed me. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Ulm encircled: Mack's army in the net.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sire, — I send my aide-de-camp. General Savary, to your Majesty in order to compliment you on your arrival. I have charged him to assure you of all my esteem, and of my desire to find opportunities of proving how ambitious I am to win your friendship. […]”
sourceTitle: To the Emperor of Russia, Linz, 1805-11-02
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: A letter to the Tsar before the shock.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think there will be no inconvenience in your coming to meet me at the Abbaye de Moelk. You can pass by Braunau where you will see General Lauriston. The Emperor of Germany is still at Vienna. He has written me several letters, and would like to come to an arrangement. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Brother,— I have received your letter of the 20th Frimaire. Negotiations continue; my army is reposing. The army of Prince Charles is close here. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 3rd Nivose. The Emperor and Prince Charles have written to me. I shall have an interview with the archduke at three leagues from Vienna. I send you a copy of my letter to the Emperor, who has written to me in the most amiable manner. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “After manoeuvring for a few days I fought a decisive battle yesterday. I defeated the combined armies commanded by the Emperors of Russia and of Germany. Their force consisted of 80,000 Russians and 30,000 Austrians. I have made about 40,000 prisoners, taken 40. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Dateline corrected from content; the decisive battle was yesterday. After the sun of Austerlitz: victory announced.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A million francs in paper will be placed at your disposal. " You will propose a plan for distributing two millions among the marshals, generals, and colonels. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I have arrived at Munich. I have arranged your marriage with the Princess Augusta. The banns have been published. This morning the princess paid me a visit, and I had a long conversation with her. You will find her portrait on the accompanying cup; but she is much better. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Italy secured by the Danube victory.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Brother, — I send you a letter for the Minister of the Treasury (M. Barbe-Marbois). You will read it, then seal it and hand it to him. I do not yet know whether it is incapacity or treason, but the coalition has had no more useful ally than this minister. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Emperor of Germany asked for an interview, which I granted; it lasted from 2 till 4 P.M. I will. you what I think of him when I see you. He wished to conclude peace on the spot. He appealed to my feelings; I defended myself, a kind of warfare which I assure you was not difficult. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I arrived here yesterday evening, and I shall leave to-morrow. I send you the Moniteur, in which you will find matters concerning yourself. " Napoleon. " P.S. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will be in the vicinity of Rome on the 15th. I have sent you the General Dumas. Marshal Massena ought to be with the army. I count that after a few days' repose you will have 40,000 men, with whom you can form three corps: Marshal Massena will command the strongest; General St. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Pressburg peace: Austria pays, Naples falls to Joseph.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will occupy Frankfort with a division of your army. At first you will levy no contribution on the city. It is only when you have united your whole army corps that you will demand 4,000,000 francs, and pay the same into the military chest of the Grand Army. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — The affairs of Cattaro are not getting settled; however, I have decided to remain in Germany until I know how matters are likely to turn out. Keep an eye on the movements of the Austrians. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Brother, — I see with pleasure that you have burned an insurgent village. I suppose that you allowed the soldiers to pillage it. That is the way in which villages which revolt should be treated. It is the right of war, and it is also a duty prescribed by policy.”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-04-22
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “After all the difficulties in the way of constructing the Arc de Triomphe on the site of the Bastille, I consent to its being constructed at the gate of Chaillot, at I'Etoile [where it now stands]. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — General Lemarois should have reached Ancona by this time. I have given him the command of the troops in the Papal States. Lemarois was an old and trusted aide-de-camp; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Sister, — I have received your letters. Do not exact any oath from the priests; it leads to nothing but difficulty. Go your own way; suppress the convents. Napoleon having caused the Concordat to be published at Lucca, and the Pope having interfered, a most violent note was the consequence. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am not at all surprised that you are satisfied with Marshal Jourdan. I was equally satisfied with him in the administration of Italy; he is an upright, active, and methodical man. " I do not see why you leave Massena at Capua. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-05-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pleasure the energy which you display in governing. The forty-four individuals condemned to death and to the galleys is a salutary measure, which will serve as an example, and will check those who desire to indulge in their natural inconstancy. NOTE. "St. Cloud, 14/ A May, 1806. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I have re-called you from Rome because it is not in accordance with my dignity that you should remain at so ill-conducted a court which does all it can to annoy me, and which I shall be constrained to punish sooner or later. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Rome and Paris: the Concordat strained.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I asked you for a note on the forces of Prussia. The information contained in the letters of Laforest is not what I want. I require to know the general situation of the army of the King of Prussia. On the 9th June, Napoleon drew up instructions for General Sebastiani: — " 1st. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Lord Yarmouth has arrived, with full powers from the King of England to sign peace. We should be tolerably well agreed but for Sicily. The English will recognise you as King of Naples, but, as you have not taken Sicily, they cannot recognise you there. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-06-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pleasure that you are satisfied with the Dutch. The pretensions of your finance minister are out of the question. My expenses are heavy, and I cannot aid you as I should like. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Holland, St.  Cloud, 1806-06-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Inform M. Alquier that I regard the Pope from a temporal and from a spiritual point of view. As a temporal prince he forms part of my confederation, whether he likes it or no. If he makes arrangements with me I shall leave him his present states; if not I shall seize on all his coasts. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We have no news from General Regnier. The art of war about which every one speaks is a difficult art; you have not a man in your council who understands the GENERAL Stuart's humanity. 245 first notions of it. I have concluded peace with Russia (treaty not ratified). […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-07-02
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is my intention to organise nine metropolitan seminaries without delay. Present me a report on the number of priests necessary. Draw attention to the necessity of having priests well educated and attached, and to the evil produced by bad theology and the disputes arising therefrom. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I thank you for what you say about my fete day. Affairs are getting settled. I will soon send you instructions for your voyage to Paris. I know that you wish to come here. You will see the Queen of Holland. We will keep the princess until after her confinement. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you a letter, which will make you thoroughly acquainted with that scamp Lucchesini. My opinion was formed long ago with respect to that wretch. He has continually deceived you, because I have long perceived that nothing is more easy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I send you a copy of the catechism, which has been adopted for France; it would be a good thing if it could be adopted for Italy without inconvenience. But it is a delicate matter, and you must be very circumspect. Consult the minister of worship. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Daughter, — I have read with pleasure your letter of the loth. You are right to rely upon my affection. Take care of yourself in your present condition, and try and not give us a daughter. I would give you a recipe for that, but you would not believe in it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I was just going to send you orders for the return of the army, when I learned that the Emperor of Russia had refused to ratify the treaty. I must wait therefore for some days to see what will happen. Send some Polish officers to the Russian frontier to see what is going on. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with surprise that the chief of the staff dares to correspond with the enemy without your permission. General Caesar Berthier is then ignorant of his duty! The reply of Sidney Smith is impertinent, as is everything which emanates from that officer. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, St.  Cloud, 1806-09-07
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You have heard of the armaments made by Prussia, and the non-ratification of Russia. My negotiations with ' England are not broken off, but they put forward the most extraordinary pretensions. They wish to have Surinam, Berbice, and all your colonies. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Holland, St.  Cloud, 1806-09-10
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Immediately after the battle of Jena the King of Prussia sent me an aide-de-camp with a letter. To-day he sends me the Marquis de Lucchesini. I have ordered. him to remain at the outposts, and I have sent Duroc to know what he wants. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have manoeuvred finely against the Prussians. Yesterday I gained a great victory. They had 150,000 men. I took 30,000 prisoners, lOO guns and standards. I was in presence and close to the King of Prussia; I nearly captured him and the queen. I have been bivouacking for two days. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Jena eve: writing Josephine before the battle.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the letter of your Royal Highness. I was much touched by the position of Madame de Hatzfeld. I convinced her that her husband was guilty, and that, according to the laws of war, he ought to be executed. However, I spared him even the disagreeableness of a trial. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: From occupied Berlin: courtesy to the defeated dynasty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have crushed the Prussian monarchy; I shall crush the Russians if they arrive. I no longer fear the. Austrians. I shall not ask you for any troops; I have no need of them. If, however, you could send me sOme cavalry, do so." We have two letters written from Potsdam on the subject of the theatre. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am at Kustrin in order to make some reconnaissances. I shall see, in two days, if you can come. Hold yourself in readiness. I hope that the Queen of Holland will be of the party. It is two o'clock in the morning. I have just risen; this is the custom of war. "NAPOLEON.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to take a town in Poland. This is the first town. This evening I shall be at Posen. After that I will call you to Berlin, so that we may arrive there on the same day. My health is good. The weather is rather bad; it has been raining for three days. My affairs are going on well. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Have a circular written, and take measures so that, throughout the extent of the empire, all letters coming from England, or written in English and by Englishmen, be seized. This is most important, as it is absolutely necessary to isolate England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Finances follow the eagles into Poland.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Prussia, which had formed a league with Russia, has disappeared. I have destroyed her armies, and am master of her strong places. " My armies are upon the Vistula, and Warsaw is in my power. "Prussian and Russian Poland are rising, and are forming armies to reconquer their independence. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The eastern alliance: Paris courts Constantinople.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I am starting for Warsaw. I shall be back in a fortnight, when I hope I shall be able to send for you. However, I should see you return to Paris, where you are desired, with pleasure. You know that I depend upon events. All my affairs are going on well. Adieu, my friend. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I laughed heartily on receiving your last letter. You have formed an idea of the belles of Poland which they do not deserve. I received your letter in a wretched. barn, having mud, wind, and straw for my bed {sic). To-morrow I shall be at Warsaw. I think that everything is finished for this year. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think that you have done wrong to create marshals, which has the inconvenience of costing money, and of giving men who have done little great pretensions. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Holland, Warsaw, 1807-01-02
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My good Friend, — I have received your letter of the 5th; what you say of your grief gives me pain. Why these tears, this chagrin.' I shall soon see you; do not doubt my sentiments; and if you wish to be still dearer to me exhibit greater strength of mind. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Turkey has declared war against Russia. A Tartar who left Constantinople on the 2nd brings me excellent news from that country. " A million has been forwarded to you from Turin. My health never was better, and the consequence is that I have become more galant than formerly. " Napoleon.”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, Warsaw, 1807-01-14

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 17th, and thank you for all you say. I am aware of your attachment, which I greatly prize. What are you doing in Paris } I have not heard that you gave a little ball during the Carnival. " Napoleon. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I beg that you will spare the states of Mecklenberg Strelitz. There is a grandmother of the Princesse Eugene there. archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must allow the Place de la Concorde to retain its present name. Concorde, this is what renders France invincible. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 3 ist December. The affair of Hesse Cassel is terminated. It appears that it was the soldiery which wished to move. « Napoleon " In fact some 10,000 Hessians refused for a time to lay down their arms. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Our affairs here could not be going on better. A corps of 20,000 men has beep cut off. The Russian army is flying it knows not where, in the greatest disorder; artillery baggage, magazines are falling into our hands. My only fear is lest the corps cut off should be Prussian corps. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — I am in pursuit of the Russian army. I have driven it from all its positions, and am going to force it back behind the Niemen. It is splendid weather, and everything is going on well. « NAPOLEON.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — There was a great battle yesterday; I gained the victory, but we have lost a great many men. The loss of the enemy, which is still more considerable, does not console me. I write these few lines to you myself, although I am very tired, to tell you that I am well and that I love you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — I send you my aide-de-camp, General Bertrand, who possesses my entire confidence. He has things to say to you which I hope will prove agreeable. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Prussia, I'^th, 1807-02-01

context: Peace offered to a beaten king.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Spread the following reports in an official manner. They are, however, true. Spread them first in the salons and then put them in the papers — that the Russian army is greatly weakened, that some regiments are reduced to 150 men. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — I congratulate you on the confinement of the princess; I am very anxious to learn that she is doing well and out of all danger. I hope that your daughter will be as good and as amiable as her mother. It remains for you now to have a boy next year. Have your daughter called Josephine. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Since the Porte refuses to have troops at Constantinople or in Bosnia, you can assure the ambassador that it shall no longer be a question of this. As for the officers asked for, it will be necessary to know the number required, their rank, and branch. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 20th. The Enghsh squadron is before Constantinople. I have received news up to the loth February, which shows that the English ambassador has left Constantinople. We shall now see how all this will end. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, OSTERODE, 1807-03-01
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have seen in the newspapers a pretended letter written in Russia. It is lamentable. We do not require to be defended by fables. No man in his senses will be deceived, and it will only create a bad effect. The Russians belonging to the army never say among themselves that they gained the battle. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The partisan SchiU has been cut off from Kolberg. That wretch, who is a sort of brigand, has fallen back on 1 Koeslin. Send some Saxon or Polish cavalry in pursuit of this wretch. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “There can be no doubt that Rear-Admiral Allemand should not attack an equal force of the enemy, much more a superior force. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The navy ordered from a Polish mill town.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Did I ever give you an order to send 10,000 Prussians to Spain 1 I told my Minister for Foreign Affairs to make such a proposal to Spain, but was that equivalent to an an order from me.'' This sort of thing has happened. several times. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Son, — Send General Lauriston twenty-five gold and silver watches to be given to the Turks. Also send twenty-five to Marmont. " Napoleon." to the king of holland. author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I must say that I was not pleased with the preamble of your order for suppressing the monasteries. With regard to all that concerns religion you must use the language of religion, and not that of philosophy. That is the great art of the person who governs. […]”
sourceTitle: To the King of Naples, FlNKENSTElN, 1807-04-14

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am delighted to hear nothing more of Madame de Stael. When I trouble myself about her it is when I have facts before me. archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The aides-de-camp of Marshal Angereau, instead of remaining with the army, have followed him to Paris. Let me know to what corps they belong, for it is not my intention to allow them to remain in Paris. "Napoleon." They might say more than was agreeable about Eylau.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It seems to me that I wrote to the Princess Pauline that she might go to the waters. I only opposed this by way of advice, because I see that the doctors order waters when they want to get rid of their patients. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have just seen the Emperor Alexander; I was well satisfied with him; he is a handsome, good, and youthful Emperor; he has more intelligence than is generally supposed. He is coming to stay at Tilsit to-morrow. " Napoleon.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “\ " I have just seen the Emperor of Russia in the middle of the Niemen on a raft where a handsome flag was hoisted. To-morrow the Emperor is going to present the King of Prussia to me, and is coming to reside here. To that effect I have neutralised the town ofTilsit. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — Desirous of placing near your Majesty some one who will be able to express to you viva voce the sentiments with which you have inspired me, I send you my aide-de-camp, the General of Division, Savary, whom I have appointed ambassador to your court. […]”

archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am proprietor, in the duchy of Warsaw, of all the debts due to the King of Prussia by private individuals. These debts are due for money advanced to proprietors on the security of their land. They appear to amount to a sum of 60,000,000 francs. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The English have disembarked at Copenhagen. They are bombarding that town. My opinion is that Russia should march an army against Sweden to force her to take part with Denmark. The Emperor Alexander has only to say what he desires and I will do all that is necessary. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send an extraordinary courier to General Junot, ordering him twenty-four hours after its reception to enter Spain with his army, and to march upon Portugal. author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send me a description of the provinces through which you pass, the roads and the nature of the ground. Send me sketches. Let the officers of engineers perform this work, which is important. Let me see the distance of the villages, the nature of the country, and its resources. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marescalchi will communicate to you the treaty which I have concluded with Spain; you will see that Tuscany belongs to me. My intention is to unite it to Italy. I think that I have troops enough at Leghorn to accomplish this. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
